title: Class 3 randomness can arise without randomness in initial conditions

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Class 3 randomness can arise without randomness in initial conditions

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The randomness of class 3 systems is not merely inherited from random initial conditions: random behavior can be generated even when the initial conditions contain no randomness at all.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the crucial point that I discovered only some time later is that random behavior can also occur even when there is no randomness in initial conditions.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 6, “Starting from Randomness”; section “Randomness in Class 3 Systems” (from p. 261), p. 261. Scope: class 3 cellular automata such as rule 30 and rule 22

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch06-14: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.88

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The central existence statement has explicit deterministic examples and can be reproduced immediately. “Random behavior” requires a statistical interpretation, but multiple standard measures can decisively distinguish it from merely inherited random input.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Evolve specified class 3 rules such as rules 30 and 22 from deterministic simple seeds and apply entropy, correlation, compressibility, and standard statistical tests to growing output windows. Strong random-like statistics from a fully fixed seed confirm the existence claim; persistent simple structure across the cited rules refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Results depend on which projection of the pattern is tested.

Statistical tests cannot prove algorithmic randomness.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.98
data adequacy: 0.82
analysis feasibility: 0.95
operationalizability: 0.76
discriminating power: 0.86

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The claim is existential and names rule 30 and rule 22, both of which are trivial to run from simple seeds, with the rule 30 center column already deposited in the OEIS. Standard batteries can confirm the practical randomness the text asserts, or expose a regularity that would undermine the example. They do not prove the absence of every possible pattern, which is why discriminating power is below the operational clarity of the simulation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Generate rule 30 and rule 22 from simple seeds, including one black cell, and apply a standard randomness battery to interior columns and rows. Passage together with no obvious nested or periodic closed form supports the existential claim; a short regular description of those sequences would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A statistical battery can miss a hidden regularity.

Random here means random under practical tests, which is the standard the book itself uses.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.68
data adequacy: 0.84
data existence: 0.92
operationalizability: 0.7
analysis feasibility: 0.9

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: If the claim holds, the centre column of rule 30 started from a single black cell (an initial condition with no randomness) passes a standard battery of statistical randomness tests as well as the centre column of rule 30 started from a random initial condition and as well as a pseudo-random reference stream, whereas a nested deterministic sequence (Thue-Morse) fails the same battery.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py generates the rule 30 centre column for 2^20 steps from a single black cell (S1) and from a seeded random row of width 2^21+1 (S2) using big-integer bit operations, a PCG64 stream (S3) and the Thue-Morse sequence (S4), checks S1 against all 100001 terms of the OEIS A051023 b-file, and applies ten NIST SP 800-22-style tests (monobit, block frequency M=128, runs, longest run M=10000, serial m=16, approximate entropy m=10, cumulative sums, DFT, Bonferroni autocorrelation over lags 1-64, 16-bit block chi-square) plus the lzma compression ratio to each. Runtime about 5 min, dominated by the two 2^20-step evolutions.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. Sequences of N = 2^20 bits: (S1) rule 30 centre column from a single black cell; (S2) rule 30 centre column from a random initial row (numpy seed 20261031, width 2N+1, so that the column is exactly the random-initial-condition case); (S3) numpy PCG64 bits, seed 20261031; (S4) the Thue-Morse sequence. Battery of 10 tests, each giving a p-value with pass meaning p >= 0.01: monobit frequency; block frequency (M = 128); runs; longest run of ones (M = 10000, K = 6); serial (m = 16, minimum of the two p-values); approximate entropy (m = 10); cumulative sums (minimum of forward and backward); discrete Fourier transform spectral test; autocorrelation (lags 1..64, Bonferroni-corrected normal p-value of the largest |r|); and a 16-bit non-overlapping block chi-square uniformity test. Also record the lzma compression ratio of the packed bits. PASS (supports) if S1 passes at least 9 of 10 tests and has lzma ratio >= 0.99, S2 and S3 each pass at least 9 of 10, S4 fails at least 4 tests, and the first terms of S1 agree exactly with the OEIS A051023 b-file over the whole length of the b-file.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes) if S1 passes 7 or fewer of the 10 tests or has lzma ratio < 0.98 (an exploitable regularity), or if S1 disagrees with OEIS A051023 (then the generator is wrong and the test is aborted as inconclusive/other). If S1 passes exactly 8, or S4 fails fewer than 4 tests (battery not discriminating), the verdict is 'mixed'. If the OEIS file cannot be fetched the OEIS cross-check is dropped and reported, and the verdict rests on the generated sequences.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: randomness tests passed (p >= 0.01) by the rule 30 single-cell centre column, out of 10

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: at alpha = 0.01 per test a truly random sequence fails at least one of 10 tests with probability about 0.10

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: 'Random behaviour' is read as the book itself reads it (practical randomness, pp. 261 and 1085 ff.): the sequence passes standard statistical tests and is incompressible, not algorithmic randomness, which no finite test can establish. 'No randomness in initial conditions' is realised by the single-black-cell seed; the book's own comparison (p. 261) is with random initial conditions, so S2 is the matched control and S4 is a control for a deterministic but nested (non-random) sequence that the battery must reject for the test to be discriminating. Rule 22 is also mentioned in the claim's context but its single-cell pattern is nested; only rule 30, the book's example on this page, is tested.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
Rule 30 centre column from a single black cell and from a random initial row, pseudo-random reference bits, and the Thue-Morse sequence, 2^20 bits each, generated by analysis.py

OEIS A051023, middle column of rule 30 from a single black cell (b-file)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Passing a finite statistical battery is practical randomness, the sense the book uses; it does not establish algorithmic randomness or exclude a regularity invisible to these tests (the sequence is of course computable).

The 16-bit block chi-square test has expected count 1 per cell, so its chi-square p-value is approximate (the true null variance of the statistic is about 1.5 times the chi-square value); the same approximation is applied to all four sequences and S1 passed it with p = 0.26.

S1's smallest p-value is 0.037 (approximate entropy, m = 10); with ten tests at alpha = 0.01 a single marginal value is expected. S2 (random initial row) had its smallest p-value at 0.018 (cumulative sums). Both rule 30 columns are statistically indistinguishable from the PCG64 stream in this battery, while Thue-Morse fails 7 of 10 tests and compresses to 0.4% of its size.

Only rule 30 was tested. Rule 22, also named in the claim's context, gives a nested pattern from a single black cell, and the book's example on p. 261 is rule 30.
